work.author: Severian of Gabala
work.title: In illud: Pater, transeat a me calix iste

paragraphs.text: Brothers, when the law of almsgiving was being preached to us, when the sermon on love for the poor and on hospitality was being worked through, I saw clearly how much all of you longed for it, and I praised your zeal and called your eagerness blessed. Like a thirsty land you seized on the heavenly word. You knew that what rain is to the earth, the word of God is to the soul. Just as rain stirs the earth to put out shoots, the word of God rouses souls to bear the fruit of a godly philosophy. This, I think, is why blessed Moses, bearing witness to the flourishing and fruitful power of divine teaching, said in that great and holy song: “Let my utterance be awaited like rain, and let my words come down like dew.” And so that he would not seem to claim for himself the authorship of so great a theology, he at once added: “For I have called on the name of the Lord.”

I praise you, brothers, because you are not excited by mere wording. You seize on the beauty of the thoughts. Like the wise bee, you enter this pure and spiritual meadow of the holy Scriptures and gather the flowers of piety, and each of you molds the divine oracles into honeycomb in the hidden workshop of the soul. Honey and honeycomb have their nature and power in the flowers, but their use and enjoyment come from the industry of the bees. In the same way, I think, the flowers of this piety and its power are found in divine Scripture, but the enjoyment of divine piety comes from the industry of the virtuous. Blessed David also molded these divine oracles into honeycomb within himself. Experience had taught him how great a good piety is, and so he cried out somewhere in his psalms: “How sweet are your words to my throat, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth!”

Yet I do not so much praise your eagerness as marvel at the abundant love of our father, which flourishes with divine wisdom and shines with heavenly grace. He is so great a river, watering so great a church and gladdening so great a city of God (“for the streams of the river make glad the city of God”), gushing with pure and clear waters, and still he welcomes the trickles of our words. He is so great a cloud, heavy with heavenly rains, and still he does not shake off the drizzle of our tongue. Instead he joins you in praising. Before you ever hear them, he supplies the speaker, through his intercession, with the things that are spoken, and then he praises what is his own as though it belonged to someone else. In this he imitates his own Master, Christ, who spoke through all the prophets and then praises what the prophets proclaimed. Christ himself spoke through Isaiah the prophet, he himself sounded forth the gift of the Spirit, and he himself approves what came from Isaiah when he says to the Jews: “Hypocrites, Isaiah spoke well about you.” It was not Isaiah who spoke well. It was you, Lord, who spoke well through Isaiah and through all the prophets. Blessed Zechariah bears witness to this when he says: “As he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets from of old.” For the words were not the prophets' own but the working of the Spirit. A pen does not write what it wants; it writes what the hand commands. In the same way the tongue of the prophets does not utter what it wants but what it is commanded, directed by the authority of the Holy Spirit. That, I think, is why blessed David rightly cries: “My tongue is the pen of a swift scribe.” So this admirable father, who grants us an abundance of speech through his holy prayers, praises as a listener what he himself supplies by praying. We have, then, so great and so eminent a father, an excellent president of this festival, who judges not by law but awards the prize by love. Come, then: let us be given wings by his holy prayers and lift our minds to the height of the glory of the Only-begotten. We do not expect to reach anything worthy of it. Nothing reaches the worth of the Only-begotten, neither breadth of speech nor depth of thought, for it surpasses every mind and every concept. David hints at this when he says: “A man shall draw near with a deep heart, and God shall be exalted.” However deep anyone goes in speaking of God, he finds the knowledge of the truth higher still.

Let us speak, then, of the goodness of the Only-begotten, starting from the passage just read. The fountain of wisdom uses parables. He who says through David, “I will open my mouth in parables,” uses parables. He sets before us an image that is full of great power, though as far as its wording goes it seems unlike his own goodness. “Which of you,” he says, “has a friend, and goes to him at midnight and says to him, ‘Friend, lend me three loaves, because a friend of mine has arrived from a journey and I have nothing to set before him’? And the other answers, ‘The door is shut, and my children are in bed with me. Do not trouble me; I cannot get up and give you anything.’” Then what does he add? “Truly, truly I say to you, even if he will not get up and give him anything because he is his friend, yet because of his shamelessness he will get up and give him more than he wants. And I say to you: ask, and it will be given to you.” What likeness does this parable bear to the abundance of God's giving? God is sleepless by nature, while the man lies in bed. God is not held back by sloth, while the man is a slave to sloth and sleep. What, then, does the mismatch in the parable mean? For he added, “And I say to you: ask,” just as that man asked the one who was asleep. Do you sleep, then, Lord? Is your nature not sleepless? Is it not about you that the prophets cry, “Behold, he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep”? What, then, does the mismatch in the parable mean? The Savior's teaching always tends both to present like things through like and to show one thing through its opposite. He does this in another parable too. Once, wishing to show by contrast the goodness that wells up from him, his abundant grace and his kindness that is never exhausted, he set out an image of the same kind as the one we have just heard. But let us first examine this one and make clear what it is meant to show. The image is indeed unlike. What the Savior means is this: if the persistence of the man waiting at the door roused one who was a slave to sleep, held fast by sloth and shut in behind a door, and if diligence overcame sloth, will not the persistence of those who truly wait on him rouse the immaterial nature, I mean God, who is held by no sloth and enslaved to no sleep? Who would dispute this meaning? And so that you may learn exactly how he showed one thing by its opposite, a little further on he used the same kind of image again, one that shows a thing through its opposite: “Which of you,” he says, “if his son asks for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, will give him a snake instead of a fish? Or if he asks for an egg, will give him a scorpion instead of an egg?” Then, setting the better beside the human by way of comparison, he says: “If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give good things to those who ask him?” Do you see how he showed one thing by setting its opposite beside it?

He uses a parable of this kind elsewhere too, as I said a moment ago. I think it good and necessary to say what that parable is and what force it has. “There was a judge in a certain city,” he says, “who did not fear God and had no regard for man.” A widow kept pestering him persistently and achieved nothing more, for his godlessness and harshness were not shamed by her pleading. Yet in the end her persistence overcame his savage severity. “And that unjust judge said to himself, ‘Even if I do not fear God or feel shame before men, still, because she keeps troubling me, shall I not grant her justice?’” That is the parable. Then the Savior, wishing once again to show one thing by its opposite, immediately added: “See what the unjust judge said. And will God not grant justice to those who cry out to him?” In other words: if the widow's persistence bent the unjust and harsh judge to compassion, will not the persistence of those who wait on him draw the good God, the loving Father, the Master who loves humankind, to mercy?

That is what he taught through that parable, and he teaches the same through the present one: “And I say to you: ask, and you will receive; knock, and it will be opened.” Like the man who knocked and said, “Friend, open,” seek and ask, and you will find. But when you ask something of God, consider what you are asking for and from whom you are asking it. For many people, brothers, take up differing views of God in their prayers. When they pray about their own sins, they want God to be good and loving toward humankind. But when they call on him to punish those who wrong them, they want him to be severe and just and full of strict judgment. For example, when someone stands up and prays for himself, he uses words meant both to persuade God and to move him: “I beseech you, Lord, have mercy on me, unworthy as I am. I beseech you, Lord: you are good, you love humankind, you overlook sins, you pass over wrongs. If you mark iniquities, Lord, who can stand before you? Deal with me according to your mercy.” Everyone says such things when praying for themselves. But when someone comes aggrieved against an enemy, he forgets this language and turns his plea in a different direction. And what does he say then? “Lord, you are a just judge; wicked deeds do not please you. Avenge me on my enemies. You are a judge of truth; do not be patient with my enemies, but as judge of truth, judge according to the truth.” God answers: “When I judge you, you want me to be good, and when I judge your enemies, you want me to be just? Have you forgotten your earlier prayers? Did you not call me good? Did you not implore me as one who loves humankind? Did you not plead with me as one who is long-suffering? What then? Shall I divide myself to suit your opinions? Shall I sell justice to suit your pleasure?” It is not possible for you to receive the good things that come from his goodness while your enemies receive the lawful penalties of his just judgment. One who is good is good toward all, and one who is just keeps justice toward all. Take care, then, that by praying against your enemies you do not set the Just One against yourself. The Just One examines your deeds along with everyone else's. So if you call on him as the just judge against your enemies, you necessarily provoke the judge against yourself as well. But if you entreat him as the good God on your own behalf, he will be good toward everyone, even if you do not want him to be. Whoever prays, then, must ask for things that please God and plead for things that give God satisfaction. The Savior said, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me,” and then added, “yet not as I will, but as you will.” If he did that, will you, a mere human being, judge by your own will and not yield to the will of God?

But now let me turn my sermon to the main subject, since I know you are demanding it of me. I see that all of you are crowded together and worn down by the strain. But Isaiah consoles you all and urges you to listen when he rightly says: “Learn to listen while you are hard pressed.” He spoke well, and all of you have listened well: hard pressed in body but refreshed in spirit. The present affliction frees you from many afflictions, and sweat shed for God's sake cures every disease of sin. When a fever breaks in a sweat, as nature produces it, bodily disease is cured. Then will not sweat shed for God and for the word of God, flowing as from a spring of longing, cure the disease of sin completely?

But let us return to our subject. I know you are demanding the explanation I left out. Many of you long for it and look for it as friends, but many others are simply hunting for phrases and trying to find fault. Everyone knows that many of these critics have spread it about that I left the passage unexamined out of weakness. What surprises me is not their accusation but its poor timing. You charge me like a lender who has not been repaid. When I was asked for the explanation, did I run away from answering? When someone else put a question to me, did I brush the question aside? I made the promise myself, and I forgot it myself. “And why did you forget?” someone asks. Then blame the weakness of human nature, and do not find fault with the explanation itself. Above all, even if the explanation were beyond me, the force of the question would surely not perish along with the weakness of my speaking. The rights of the truth are not betrayed by my feebleness. In this case the reason for the delay is plain. The sheer number of things I had said pulled my mind this way and that like waves, and drew me away from the question I had set out.

So what I left out unwillingly, I now willingly pay back. Yet even as I repay the debt, I am afraid again. I find in you a new and strange kind of drunkenness, one that produces not forgetfulness but awakens memory, though we all know that drunkenness wipes out memory and brings forgetfulness in its place. But you, brothers, the more you are made drunk by the divine word, the more you banish forgetfulness and show a godly memory. And the remarkable thing is that those who pour the wine for you get drunk themselves, weighed down by the sheer burden of thought, while you, after draining so many bowls of the divine word, are still thirsty even when drunk, and you demand with great precision what was left out. One can truly hear the words of spiritual drunkards: “He skipped the cup! He did not explain the cup! He did not give us the meaning of the cup!” I love you for longing for the cup of Christ. I love you for seeking what was left out. I love you because, in that most beautiful drunkenness, you refuse to give up even a single cup, and quite rightly. At a bodily feast, the person who passes up a cup out of self-discipline is admirable. But at the divine and heavenly table, the one who passes up nothing that leads to the drunkenness of salvation, who is fed and yet hungry, drunk and yet thirsty, is truly filled with the salvation of the cup. So I count blessed in my heart both those who speak and those who listen. Those who listen are blessed when they listen with thirst, for “Blessed,” says the Savior, “are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled.” Those who speak are blessed because the divine teaching must ring in living ears, for “Blessed is he who speaks into the ears of those who listen.”

Enough of that for now. Let the text be stated, then: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.” This saying is full of many difficulties, and it causes the heretics a great deal of sickness, not because it was badly said but because it is badly understood. Some take “if it is possible” to mean something that cannot be broken, and so bring in the necessity of what they call fate and of the fabled power of the stars at birth. Others insult the dignity of the Only-begotten in a different way: from this saying they construct a servile subordination of the Son to the Father. “Because he was subject to the Father's authority,” they say, “he used this plea.” What argument, then, will suit our inquiry? Who will resolve for us this much-talked-about question of the heretics? There is no other way than to learn the truth from the truth itself. Come, then, let us climb back up to the very summit of God the Savior, to the economy itself. He does and says everything not only in keeping with the dignity that befits him but also in keeping with the economy that suits us. To be brief (for I like to be brief and to cover much in a few words): the Savior knew in advance that the passion was necessary, that a cross would be set up for the salvation of the world, that death would be exposed, and that the resurrection would be brought about. He knew this so well that he foretold it to his disciples: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be handed over into the hands of sinful men, and they will mock him and crucify him, and on the third day he will rise.” This is the voice of God foreseeing what is to come, of God anticipating experience by his knowledge, of God ordering human affairs. When he says this, Peter, out of concern to spare his flesh, protests: “God forbid, Lord! This shall never happen to you.” What does the Savior do? He is indignant at this ill-timed attitude, rebukes this ill-timed sparing, and says to him: “Get behind me, Satan, for you are not thinking the things of God but the things of men.” Here examine the whole passage carefully and consider this: if you make yourself a slave to the bare wording, you charge the Savior not only with great weakness but also with inconsistent thinking. “Lord, do you rebuke Peter for praying that the cross be kept from you, and then ask for the very thing you rebuked?” That is not only unfitting for God; it does not even become a steady man. Who would praise a general who threatens the enemy with great boldness and daring before the battle, but runs away at its very height and is exposed as a coward and a weakling? Before Christ came to his passion, he said to the one who prayed that the passion be kept from him: “Get behind me, Satan, for you are not thinking the things of God.” Does he then take up that very prayer as his own? What folly, or rather what madness, on the part of those who are slaves to the bare wording, who dare anything lightly and try to twist the meaning of divine things! They will not even consider this: that by taking the words in their bare sense they are bent on showing him to be not only inferior to the Father but also lesser than many wise and righteous people, lacking even the ordinary steadiness of human beings. What wise or righteous person, or anyone else known for virtue, denies his own virtue and dishonors the courage he has promised and proclaimed beforehand? Who is so fickle and changeable that he makes bold promises and then thinks otherwise once he is put to the test? Would the one who threatens death and the destruction of death, the one who announces the resurrection, beg to be excused from the cross? I have said these things to refute those who are slaves to the wording, who insult the Lord and peddle the truth. What, then, is the meaning of this contradiction in the words, when the truth is always in agreement with itself? What does the harmony of the truth intend, set against the conflict of the words? For the words really do conflict, but the divine meanings remain in harmony. So it is right for me to set out diligently the solution to the meanings before us, and for you to listen eagerly.

As the Lord came to the cross, the mighty God and only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords, foresaw the completion of the economy. He also foresaw how many heretics would rise up against the truth, setting aside the divine passion and falsely calling the drama of the economy something unreal. Above all he foresaw the disciples of the man named after madness, I mean the Manichaeans, who dare to say that Christ underwent the passion as a kind of shadow and appearance, that he did not even take on flesh, and that he accepted the cross too only in outward form, shadow and appearance. Because of this heretical error he stopped the heretics' mouths in advance. To show that he had put on this body that is subject to many sufferings, that agonizes, that trembles at the violence of death, that is grieved and troubled at the end of life, he says: “Now my soul is troubled,” and “My soul is very sorrowful, even to death.” Pay close attention: “My soul is very sorrowful”; “Father, if it is possible, let it pass.” If what happened was shadow and appearance, why is he troubled? If it was outward form and appearance, why is he distressed? Nothing anywhere frightens a shadow. Where there is outward form and not reality, nothing can cause distress.

Would you like me to establish the truth of this principle for you from a story? Angels once entered Sodom. They were men in appearance but angels in nature. The Sodomites tried to force them, as if they were men, into shameful and boundless lewdness. What did the angels do? Because they knew that the body they had put on could not be subjected to violence, they were not troubled. The angels' nature remained undisturbed and received no storm from the passions of the body. Lot, though, thought they really were men. He was distressed that they might suffer violence, and he pleaded with the frenzied men: “I beg you, do not wrong these men; do not let them suffer violence, since they have come under the shelter of my roof. I give up what is my own treasure: take my daughters.” What noble hospitality, to give up its own before those of strangers! But Lot was distressed because he was a man, while the nature of angels undergoes no distress. The angels came out with great authority. They took hold of the one who could suffer violence, and they struck with blindness those who had launched into that boundless, or rather godless, lewdness. These men wandered about all night looking for the door and could not find it, for those who looked with wicked eyes were rightly and justly blinded. Why am I telling you this? The ancient story has nothing in common with the present one, except this: it shows that where there is mere form, there is no fear at all, but where there is reality, there is both fear and grief. And above all, brothers, so that the Savior himself might explain whose words these were, cut off the heretics' notions and fix firmly the doctrines of the truth, he says to the apostles: “The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak.” So he himself ascribes it to the weakness of the flesh, while you, heretic, throw this lowliness onto the authority of the Godhead. Because you made no effort to get past the word and find the meaning, you have been caught insulting the Master beyond measure. You think you are proving only that he prayed to the Father and that, as one who pleads, he is lower than the one he pleads with. But I will show more clearly that if you make yourself a slave to the bare wording, you will make him not only lower than the Father but also lesser than his own apostles.

Think of those who misread "I do not speak on my own; the Father has given me a commandment about what to say and what to speak." Against them the authority of the apostle stepped forward to muzzle their madness, when Paul says, "Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord, but I give my opinion" — and he does give it. (O how much more bitter the doctrine of the heresy becomes! If Paul was allowed to exercise authority without a command from God, while Christ was not allowed to say anything outside his Father's commandments...) Just so, here too one could set the courage of the apostles beside the Lord's words and show that the heretics' madness drags the Lord's voice down far below the dignity of an apostle. But as I have often said before, if we make ourselves slaves to the wording, we fall into blasphemy; if we accept the sense, the truth remains unwounded — or rather, we remain unwounded, for the truth cannot be wounded. So if you do not grasp the deeper meaning but follow the bare wording, you will find Christ playing the coward and speaking far beneath both his own dignity and the courage of the apostles. "Now my soul is troubled." When Paul was staying in the regions of Palestine, a prophet named Agabus came and said, "Thus says the Holy Spirit: the man who owns this belt the elders and the priests in Jerusalem will bind like this." All the brothers begged Paul not to go up to Jerusalem. That noble voice, or rather that brave and noble soul, answered those who were trying to turn him back: "What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be bound but even to die for the name of Christ." Then does Paul speak with such boldness, such composure, such daring, trampling on death and on the terrors of death, while Paul's Master says, "Now my soul is troubled"? Is Paul's heart not broken, while Christ's soul is troubled? Paul says, "Not only that, but we also boast in our afflictions." Paul boasts in afflictions, but Christ, Paul's Master, says, "My soul is very sorrowful." What has sorrow in common with boasting? A mere human being counts suffering as grounds for boasting. Does Christ, who gives him strength, count the dispensation a cause of sorrow?

Consider another of Paul's attitudes, also full of great courage. He was once seized at Philippi in Macedonia, many blows were laid on him, and great affliction pained his body: "When they had laid many blows on them, they threw them into prison and fastened their feet in the stocks." Yet that noble champion of godliness, and Silas with him, overcame misfortune by strength and overcame suffering by philosophy. The historian marked this well when he wrote: "About midnight Paul and Silas were singing hymns to God." They suffer and give thanks; they are beaten and sing hymns. Note the historian's precision. He did not say, "About midnight Paul and Silas were praying to God," but "were singing hymns." Prayer often springs from affliction, but a hymn springs from exultation. So the apostles let their joy show through: "About midnight Paul and Silas were singing hymns to God" — the sign of a cheerful soul. The saints, wishing to display the cheerfulness of their souls, did not suffer, he says, like people in affliction, but sang hymns like people exulting. So Paul and Silas, who were human by nature, are great-souled in their sufferings. And will you apply to Christ, the King of the saints, lowly words that were spoken by way of dispensation, in order to pull down his dignity? Away with such a notion! Let no one insult what is holy, let no one slander what is divine, and let no one try to build impiety out of the Savior's words by reckoning them lowly.

But my listener demands that I go on. "You have shown well," he says, "that these words truly belong to the dispensation. But explain to me what the dispensation actually means here. Why did he use such words at all? Why did he say, 'Let the cup pass from me, if it is possible'?" The phrase "if it is possible," brothers, does not bring in the compulsion of fate or of the fabled horoscope, nor does it accuse the speaker of cowardice or unmanliness. "If it is possible" belongs to one who is carrying out his human role and sparing those who were going to be scandalized. He knew that the passion could scandalize many, especially those who did not know the mysteries of the dispensation: "For we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Greeks." So he who orders all things wisely took up the human image and said, in effect: if it is possible for the dispensation to be fulfilled in some other way and to come about without death, so that the many are not scandalized by such a passion — if it is possible, then, let it pass.

"But you have forced the meaning," he says. "Show me proof that he said these things to spare human weakness." Then listen to how he speaks to the apostles at that same time, at the very height of the passion: "Pray." But they dozed off. Then he reproaches them: "So you could not keep awake for one hour? Pray that you may not enter into temptation." He did not say "that I may not enter," because the passion did not harm him; it was a stumbling block for the others. "Pray that you may not enter into temptation." He did not say "that I may not enter into temptation," but "that you may not enter into temptation." It is as if he said: I am sparing you, not exempting myself from the passion. I know what is to come. I know the benefit that will blossom from the dispensation for all people. But since what you see scandalizes you before the outcome arrives, I wish the passion to be turned aside, if that is really possible.

So "if it is possible" does not mean what many think. The statement has to be worked out: it implies no inviolable necessity and no inexorable decree. Do you want to learn, brother, that his lot was not imposed on the Savior from above by necessity, but that the all-wise dispensation of the Lord himself fulfills everything by his own purpose? Hear plainly how the Lord himself got in first and dissolved the suspicion of necessity, and made known that his purpose was his own to command. Hear what he says: "No one takes my life from me." For he says, "I have authority to lay down my life, and I have authority to take it up." And again: "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." If you have authority, then, why did you use the words "if it is possible"? For your sake, you who are weak, not for mine, who am powerful and strong and above all weakness.

But why does he call the passion a cup at all? This raises a further question: why does he name the passion a cup? Scripture has always liked to call the discipline that God brings on sinners a cup. Pay close attention, I beg you, and be an intelligent listener: do not snatch at the words before I have finished, but wait for the meaning. Someone who listens badly may well misinterpret badly what is said. Still, whoever speaks in church should not be surprised if he suffers some slander from people who are simply out to misrepresent him. The apostles too were slandered as having said forbidden things. Hear Paul proclaim the slander spread against him: "And why not, as we are slandered and as some claim that we say, 'Let us do evil so that good may come'? Their condemnation is just." It is just because they misrepresent what they never heard as though they had heard it, and they bring up against their teachers things they never heard from them in order to slander them. But let us return to our subject. As I was saying, Scripture has always liked to call the disciplines or punishments that God brings on sinners a cup. But let not the enemy and spy pounce on the statement at once and say, "What then? Did Christ sin and undergo punishment for sins?" Certainly not. He himself owed no punishment; it is we who are liable to punishment. For us, who were condemned by sin and liable to punishment, he accepted death, as Isaiah too foretells: "For the sins of the people he came to death." Since, then, he received the punishment due to sinners and took it upon himself, he rightly calls it a cup. For "Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world," and "He himself bears our sins," and "for the sins of the people he was led to death."

So his passion is called a cup, for the reason given above. That is why blessed David, describing the judgment on sinners, says: "A cup in the hand of the Lord, full of unmixed wine, full of mixture; all the sinners of the earth shall drink it." And again the Lord, threatening the nations with punishment, says to Jeremiah: "Take a cup and mix it, and make all the nations and Jerusalem drink it, and say to them: Drink and be drunk and be beside yourselves." What does "be beside yourselves" mean? God's discipline drives many out of their senses. The punishment he brings often leaves many at a loss, especially when they see the righteous taken along with the unrighteous. That is what people are now repeating all over the earth: Why were priests slaughtered at the altars? Why were holy virgins carried off? Why have such terrible outrages happened? Why did God not protect his own? Since such sufferings drive people out of their senses and leave their minds perplexed, he rightly says: drink and be drunk and call quietly [?]; wait for my weakness [?], and I will lay the truth bare for you. Again, the Savior calls his own passion a cup when he says to James and John: "Can you drink this cup that I am about to drink?" — that is, can you undergo the passion I am about to undergo? They say, "Yes."

Blessed David taught clearly that "cup" means death suffered for godliness, for he says: "What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?" He is like a grateful servant who sees consolations overflowing with benefits and wants to give back some small token of gratitude himself. Think of a poor man about to receive a rich guest. He is at a loss over what to prepare for the rich man's feast, what to bring to the table that is worthy of his rank. He is often perplexed and talks to himself: How shall I receive him worthily? What shall I do? What shall I offer? How shall I honor him? How shall I entertain him? In the same way blessed David looked at human poverty and at the wealth of God's goodness, saw that nothing worthy of God can be offered by human beings, and spoke in the voice of perplexity: "What shall I render to the Lord?" I find nothing worthy of his kindness. What shall I render? What shall I do? What shall I become? With what gifts shall I repay my benefactor? When he was at a loss in everything, he found one thing, worthy not of God's kindness but of his own eagerness: "I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord." Then, since this saying was unclear and shadowy, he explained the cup by what follows. Having said, "I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord," he adds: "Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his holy ones."

So "Father, if it is possible, let the cup pass from me" means: if it is possible, let the passion pass. But you already have the answer to these questions: "if it is possible" fulfills the role of the human dispensation. The one who said this in the person of his humanity had already said, from the divinity that holds authority over all things: "I have authority to lay down my life, and I have authority to take it up again." To show that it was not the divinity that declined the passion but the weakness of the flesh, the same one says again: "The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak." And he himself made known to the disciples that the passion did not harm him but was a stumbling block for others, when he said: "Pray that you may not enter into temptation." Besides, he also teaches us this about prayer: not to demand from God everything we pray for, but to yield to his judgment. Ordering all this wisely, he says: "Not as I will, but whatever you will." These words do not befit him, but they suit you, so that when you pray you do not ask for whatever you yourself want, but yield to God's will. So when you pray, you too should say, in imitation of Christ, who humbled himself for your sake: "Yet what you will, Lord." Yield to God's will. Do not demand what goes against his purpose, for "for those who love God all things work together for good" — even what does not turn out as we wish and what happens against our intention.

We know, then, that the cup God brings is punishment for sinners, but that for Christ the passion was not a matter of punishment but of dispensation. The sinless one endured the death of sinners in order to rescue the whole world, which had been condemned by sin. "But why," someone asked, "does he call death a cup at all?" The testimony of Scripture has clearly established that the cup signifies punishment and death. But why call the passion a cup at all? A cup has nothing in common with death. The answer, brothers, is that the disciplines brought upon us seem harsh, severe, and full of misfortune. So divine Scripture has good reason to call sufferings a cup: to show that God does not punish like a severe judge or destroy without mercy, but heals our ailments like a physician and gives his disciplines to the sick like a bitter antidote. This saving cup of disciplines is bitter to the taste but excellent in its outcome. Through the image of the cup, then, the word presents the good God as a good teacher: as a father who disciplines, not as a king who condemns; not as an enemy who strikes, but as a physician who applies astringent medicine. Brothers, when a physician applies the knife or the cautery to the body, he is not fighting the person but resisting the disease. In the same way, when God brings his disciplines, he is not punishing his own creature but purging away sin. Have you ever seen a physician operate out of anger? Have you ever seen him apply the cautery, or anything else, out of anger? And yet, for the person being operated on, is not even the sight of the physicians frightening, though the healer's intention is good? The physician does not treat in anger just because the treatment frightens the patient.

Even if the practice of this art is frightening, blessed Paul spoke well and admirably for everyone when he set out a definition of discipline: "All discipline seems for the present to bring not joy but pain." When a sick man sees the physician cutting, he often pushes him away as frightening and hostile. But once he is healed, he reveres the man he used to turn from at the sight. Or do we not know, brothers, how often the severity of a disease drives the patient even to insult those who are treating him? Yet the physician forgives him in his anger, for the insult comes not from his will but from his suffering. And when he goes out adorned with health, he even pays a fee for that harshness he once imagined, and pays it not because he is asked but because he asks it of himself. So it is with us. Now we are vexed by our afflictions, but when the fruit of affliction arrives, we will praise our benefactor and marvel at him, and we too will say with David: "We went through fire and water, and he brought us out into refreshment."

And yet here he calls afflictions a cup, and not simply a cup, but a cup "in the hand of the Lord, of unmixed wine, full of mixture." Once more the saying seems self-contradictory, as far as the wording goes, for mixed and unmixed have nothing in common. Why, then, is God's cup both unmixed and mixed? The covenant [?] and discipline he always brings on human beings is both unmixed and mixed. It is unmixed because injustice is not mixed with justice, because nothing lawless, unjust, or spurious is blended into his righteous judgment. It is like unmixed wine: the eye of justice is bare and pure, and sees things clear and bright. That is why it is "a cup in the hand of the Lord of unmixed wine": injustice is not mixed with what is just. Nothing contrary is there that could corrupt the judge's truth. It is a cup of unmixed wine. Why, then, is it "full of mixture"? Does the saying not seem self-contradictory to you? Yet it agrees with the truth. As I have often said, the cup is unmixed because it holds no injustice, but it is also mixed, because compassion is mixed with justice. It is as if someone said: unmixed for retribution and mixed for compassion. For in disciplining he shows mercy, and in showing mercy he disciplines.

Now see a strange rule of truth. When God disciplines sinners, it is a sign of his providence and his love for humankind. When he does not discipline the sinner, it is a sign of his wrath and indignation. That is when you should fear God as one who hates you and turns away from you: when you sin and he does not discipline you. "For the Lord disciplines the one he loves, and he scourges every son whom he receives." But the one he turns away from because of the excess of his sin, he leaves undisciplined and unpunished. What saying proves this? Hear him say it through the prophet Hosea: "Because you have transgressed my law," he says, "I will not punish your daughters when they play the harlot." It is as if he were saying: I give you over to sin. I do not punish the lawlessness. I do not check the corruption. I do not heal the wounds of sin. I let you die in your wickedness. Do you see how his threat, in his indignation, is that he will not discipline? But when he truly loves, he does not refuse to discipline.

We have shown, then, brothers, as far as we are able, what manner of prayer this was and what "Father, if it is possible, let the cup pass from me" means: that the words did not belong to divine authority but to the human dispensation. For the Lord clearly ascribed the lowly traits of cowardice, fear, and turmoil to the weakness of the flesh when he said: "The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak." I will remind you of this saying often, to confirm the true meaning. If anyone dares to object to the explanation given for this question, let him first set out his own definition and then fight against ours, if he is able to wage war on the divine word. Let him not slander like an enemy, but bring his case into the open as one fighting for the truth. But enough of this. Let us come to the matter before us and bring the sermon to a close. I believe a complete and finished account has been given of the dispensation and of the saying. If someone still contradicts it after so much testimony, the truth has not been overturned. "If anyone," says the apostle, "is inclined to be contentious, we have no such custom." We have learned to follow the Scriptures, not to practice dialectic. I would rather commit solecisms with the Scriptures than play the Platonist with you.

Let this be enough on that subject. Now let us remember the poor. Paul clearly reminded us of them today. After saying, "Peter and James and John gave me and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship, so that we would go to the Gentiles and they to the circumcised," he added: "Only that we should remember the poor." So let us too remember the poor. Remember a poor man, and you have remembered yourself. In showing mercy to another, you show mercy to yourself. In doing good to the needy, you do good to yourself. You sow in him and reap in heaven. Almsgiving is sown here and reaped in heaven. Do not say: "What can I do, overwhelmed as I am by want? I want to give alms, but I cannot. I want to, but my straitened circumstances will not let me." Do what you can; act within your means. Learn not only to listen when you are hard pressed, but also to show mercy when you are hard pressed. Hear what Isaiah says: "To the hungry from your soul" — that is, from what you are about to eat. If you take some of it and give it, and make the needy man a sharer in your food, then by feeding him you have shown mercy to yourself. I know that you also remember what I told you about almsgiving before. Almsgiving wins friendship with God, almsgiving brings forgiveness of sins, almsgiving even rescues from death. Blessed Tabitha was handed over to death by the law of nature, but through the thanksgiving of widows she was called back from death to life. The tears of the poor broke open the gates of death. Consider what a poor man can do when he prays. When that Tabitha died, she who was full of good works, all the widows stood around Peter weeping, and the tears of the poor quenched the grief, or rather overcame the violence of death. She who had died by the law of nature was given back by the word of grace, for she was full of almsgiving. The widows wept and moved God. Pay close attention here. To die is according to nature, but to rise from the dead is both contrary to nature and above nature. If, then, the tears of the poor could accomplish what is above nature, will they not accomplish what is according to nature? Consider how much power a widow has when she groans against a powerful man. If a poor man groans against a violent rich man, if an orphan groans against those who wrong him, see how he rouses God. So do not let a needy man groan against you, do not let a poor man groan, do not let an orphan cry out against you. Sow alms among orphans, so that you may store up compassion for yourself and for your children.

Imitate Abraham, who opened his heart in hospitality to all the needy and left his descendants a pledge of salvation. And see the marvel: because he loved hospitality, he was counted worthy to welcome even the angels of God. Through hospitality he received angels too. And so [?] "man ate the bread of angels." This is how hospitality advances: by welcoming human beings it comes to welcome angels, and further still it comes to welcome God. For it was God who came, escorted by angels. That is why our Lord Jesus, the only-begotten Word of God, setting out the reward of a friendly table, says: "Whoever receives you receives me." Through hospitality blessed Abraham, too, received God.

And see the wonder of it. He saw three, yet he worshipped one, for he did not say "Lords" but "Lord." He saw three, and he praised one Lord. But this is not the time to examine those matters; it is the time to train ourselves in hospitality. He welcomed them, and he did not give them rest [?]. Strange are the mysteries of God's love for humankind! See how the One who loves humankind repays kindness: "I am the bread that came down from heaven." You feed human beings; I give heavenly food to your descendants. Contrary to the nature of angels, the angels eat what humans provide; contrary to human nature, humans receive the things of heaven. That food was not suited to the nature of angels, nor is this food suited to the nature of human beings. But now is not the time to speak of these things in detail. As for you, long for the reward of hospitality, strive for riches there, and store up the reward for yourself. You have a field: sow it in the farmland of the poor. "He scattered abroad, he gave to the poor; his righteousness endures forever." Let this be enough from us. For this reminder about the poor was given once again to confirm you, not to teach you something new. What has already been said is enough to rouse those of good will. But let us also call to mind our spiritual father, the teacher of the church, and say to him, as is fitting: "Awake, my glory! Awake, harp and lyre!" We need your teaching and your fatherly words to set the seal on what we have said. For even if there is plenty of flour, a little leaven is still needed; and even if there are many words, spiritual help is still needed, to reinforce and confirm what we have said, to the glory of Christ, for to him be glory forever and ever. Amen.
